title: The worm grew a new brain. Did the memory survive?
hook: A flatworm can grow a new brain after its old one is cut off. Some experiments say earlier training still affects the regenerated animal.
simple: The tail loses the original brain but keeps nerve cords in the rest of the body. A few studies find traces of earlier training after the head grows back, while a major 2026 replication effort could not reliably produce the learning effect at all.
why_interesting: The real question is not ‘memory without a brain.’ It is how much of the old nervous system—or some other changed tissue—must survive for past experience to bias a new brain.
tangible_edge: Regeneration gives researchers a rare way to remove candidate memory stores piece by piece. If the effect is real, the next experiment is not another dramatic decapitation; it is finding the smallest surviving tissue that still carries the bias.
why_here: Memory-blind received-wisdom check: a famous claim becomes more scientifically interesting when the experiment is reframed around assay reliability and causal localization of the surviving state.
confidence: moderate that some planarian training paradigms can leave post-regeneration behavioral effects; low-to-moderate that current evidence establishes associative memory through regeneration; very low on any specific non-neural storage mechanism

title: A tree can date history more precisely than it records the sky
hook: A solar storm can leave a date mark in tree rings. That mark helped pin Norse activity in Newfoundland to 1021.
simple: Rare bursts of solar particles change the amount of radioactive carbon in the atmosphere. Trees record that change as they grow, so a known burst can anchor an otherwise undated ring sequence to the calendar.
why_interesting: Trees do not record the burst perfectly. Different species can smear it across different rings, yet the pattern can still be precise enough to date human activity to one year.
tangible_edge: This separates two jobs we often treat as the same: measuring an event accurately and using it as a timestamp. A messy sensor can still be an excellent clock if its pattern is distinctive enough.
why_here: Expectation violation: exact-year archaeology emerges from an imperfect biological recorder because precision is earned by replicated fingerprint matching, dendrochronological crossdating and ring counting rather than by a universally identical spike ring.
confidence: high that well-characterized cosmogenic events can anchor suitable tree-ring chronologies to calendar years; high that physiology and atmospheric transport alter signal shape; moderate on how broadly subannual corrections are required across different events and species

title: Build the pressure, not the outcome
hook: A few hundred tiny organisms and two foods may be enough to watch one population split into different survival strategies.
simple: Give organisms limited energy, two competing food sources, reproduction, mutation and death. Do not score them. Let survival and reproduction decide which traits spread.
why_interesting: Complexity can come from the pressure itself. When a successful strategy changes the environment, it can accidentally make room for a different strategy.
tangible_edge: OWR can rewind the exact population just before a lucky mutation, remove it, and run hundreds of alternate futures. That turns ‘evolution happened’ into a better question: how replaceable was this exact accident?
why_here: User-directed simulation design report connecting artificial-life research to OWR's existing causal replay and sparse-search machinery, including experiments the current question-first discovery architecture is likely to miss.
confidence: high on the minimal Darwinian ingredients and resource-driven frequency dependence; moderate on which small substrate will yield the richest OWR regimes; low on any claim of sustained open-ended evolution

title: Air-pollution filters can contain a second, unread measurement
hook: Some air-pollution stations have been collecting wildlife DNA by accident.
simple: Air filters trap tiny biological particles along with pollution. Researchers can extract DNA from the same filters and identify some of the plants, animals, fungi and other organisms that contributed material.
why_interesting: Existing infrastructure can contain a second dataset nobody designed it to collect.
tangible_edge: The most interesting target may be old filter archives. One Swedish station preserved enough DNA to reconstruct decades of ecological change—but its unusually high air volume and careful storage mean we first need to learn which archives are actually usable.
why_here: Bridge between atmospheric infrastructure and biodiversity monitoring, with a retrospective archive effect that turns routine environmental sampling into latent ecological observation.
confidence: high that existing air-monitoring networks can collect useful biodiversity eDNA; high that one Swedish archive preserved multi-decade ecological signal; moderate on broad transferability across other historical filter archives

title: A Faraday cage is not an AI containment strategy
hook: A Faraday cage blocks some radio leaks. It does not block every way a computer can affect the outside world.
simple: An air-gapped computer can still leak information through magnetic fields, sound, light, power lines and other physical effects if a receiver is nearby. More importantly, any text or code we intentionally let out is already a high-bandwidth channel.
why_interesting: The containment boundary is not the metal box. It is every path by which internal state can change something an outsider can observe.
tangible_edge: The hardest channel may be the one we cannot remove: useful output. A perfectly sealed model is easy to contain and nearly useless; a useful model is allowed to communicate, so containment becomes a problem of limiting what that communication can accomplish.
why_here: User-directed side report on the physical and information-theoretic limits of containing capable LLM agents.
confidence: high that multiple physical covert-channel classes and software sandbox escapes are real; moderate on how much specific physical-channel risk survives high-assurance facility engineering; no public evidence found here that an LLM has independently invented a physical air-gap channel from a sealed machine

title: How AI subscriptions become shadow APIs
hook: Some open-source gateways turn individual AI subscriptions into pooled API capacity.
simple: They log into subscription-backed products, route requests through one or more accounts, and expose the result behind a normal API. Some uses are just alternate clients; pooling or reselling one person’s allowance is the clearer abuse pattern.
why_interesting: Flat subscriptions assume one human uses one seat. Agents can consume that allowance continuously, so a personal subscription can start behaving like wholesale compute.
tangible_edge: The cleanest design line is not ‘official app versus third-party app.’ It is who benefits from the entitlement. GitHub already allows third-party Copilot apps when every user brings their own account; the trouble starts when one entitlement becomes capacity for strangers.
why_here: User-directed side report on the increasingly important boundary between flat-rate AI subscriptions and machine-speed programmable inference.
confidence: high that subscription-to-API gateways and provider enforcement are substantial and active; moderate on how much traffic is commercial re-serving; low on any public estimate of market share

title: The hot-hand problem has an opponent in it
hook: A shooter who keeps making shots does not face the same next shot. The defense reacts.
simple: NBA tracking studies show defenders change pressure and shooters take different shots after recent success. That means the next attempt is partly shaped by the streak itself.
why_interesting: A hot-hand test can confuse two things: whether the shooter changed and whether the opponent changed the conditions.
tangible_edge: This is bigger than basketball. In any adaptive contest, success changes the measurement environment. The better you perform, the more the system may work to make your next result harder.
why_here: Bridge between sports statistics and adaptive-system measurement: competitive performance changes the environment that produces the next measurement.
confidence: high that defenses and shot environments respond to recent shooting success; moderate on the size and generality of the 2026 closest-defender effect; unresolved on the existence and size of a latent in-game hot-hand effect

title: Earth's ‘missing lead’ may be partly a model problem
hook: Earth’s rocks seem to be missing the kind of old lead that a simple model says should still exist.
simple: Uranium slowly turns into lead. When geologists compare lead isotopes in accessible rocks with a simple model of Earth’s history, the numbers do not balance.
why_interesting: A new deep-mantle storage mechanism makes hidden lead plausible, but another line of work says the original bookkeeping problem may have been too simple.
tangible_edge: Both discoveries can be useful at once: there may be places deep Earth can hide unusual lead, while better models reduce how much hidden lead we need to invent in the first place.
why_here: Vocabulary trapdoor: the ‘missing lead paradox’ turns a familiar element into a problem about planetary isotope bookkeeping, inaccessible reservoirs and model assumptions.
confidence: high on the classical isotope imbalance and direct unradiogenic mantle observations; moderate on the importance of pressure-stable Pb-S storage; low on any claim that one hidden reservoir uniquely solves the global Pb budget

title: We cleaned up ship fuel. The clouds noticed.
hook: Cleaning sulfur out of ship fuel changed clouds over the ocean.
simple: Ship exhaust used to release more sulfur particles. Those particles can make some marine clouds brighter. A 2020 fuel rule sharply cut the sulfur source, giving researchers a rare before-and-after test.
why_interesting: An air-pollution rule accidentally became a climate experiment.
tangible_edge: The visible white ‘ship tracks’ were only a small part of the cloud effect in at least one study. The obvious signal may be the biased tip of a much larger invisible response.
why_here: Expectation violation: an air-quality rule became a rare real-world perturbation of cloud microphysics, with consequences that are more scientifically useful than the shallow 'cleaner air caused warming' headline.
confidence: high on the sign of the sulfur-cloud perturbation and post-2020 emissions change; moderate on exact global forcing magnitude; low-to-moderate on attribution of specific recent temperature anomalies

title: A body can keep cells from another person for decades
hook: Pregnancy can leave a tiny population of another person’s cells in your body for decades.
simple: Cells cross the placenta in both directions. Some fetal-origin cells remain in mothers, and some maternal-origin cells remain in children long after pregnancy.
why_interesting: One body can contain small, long-lived cell populations with another person’s genome.
tangible_edge: The open question is not whether the cells are there; it is what controls which ones survive. Mouse work suggests later pregnancies can replace older microchimeric populations, so the body may be managing a changing cell ecology rather than storing a permanent scrapbook.
why_here: Memory-blind hidden mechanism: a mature biological phenomenon far outside the recent feed whose established facts are strange enough on their own, with an active measurement and population-dynamics frontier.
confidence: high on bidirectional long-term persistence; moderate-to-low on general functional effects and on whether mouse population replacement dynamics generalize to humans

title: Which version of the past does a smell belong to?
hook: You can faithfully recreate how an old object smells today and still get its historical smell wrong.
simple: Researchers can analyze odor molecules and test reconstructions with people. That can preserve a smell, but it does not automatically tell you which moment in the object’s life you have preserved.
why_interesting: Smell has its own version of patina. Aging changes the object, so ‘authentic’ can mean the smell now or the smell when it was new.
tangible_edge: A museum recreating a 200-year-old perfume has to choose a timestamp before it chooses a formula. The historical question comes before the chemistry.
why_here: Memory-blind field discovery: olfactory heritage sits far outside the recent research neighborhood and exposes an unfamiliar archival problem with current chemistry, museum practice and living-tradition consequences.
confidence: high that olfactory heritage is a real interdisciplinary practice and that bounded scent reconstruction can be rigorously validated; moderate on how well these methods generalize to complex or vanished smellscapes

title: What survives after the genome doesn't
hook: When ancient DNA is gone, tooth enamel can still hold a few useful pieces of molecular information.
simple: Enamel traps a small set of proteins while teeth form. Those proteins carry much less information than DNA, but some survive far longer and can reveal things like sex or evolutionary relationships.
why_interesting: There is no single molecular expiration date for fossils. DNA, proteins, isotopes and anatomy disappear at different rates.
tangible_edge: A fossil can be ‘too old for DNA’ without being molecularly silent. That changes which museum specimens are worth sampling and which evolutionary questions can still be asked.
why_here: Memory-blind capability shift: a mature technique outside the recent technology-heavy research neighborhood that materially changes which questions can be asked of old fossils.
confidence: high that enamel palaeoproteomics is a real and expanding molecular method; moderate on how broadly it will scale across collections and deep-time preservation regimes

title: The internet can contain a connection nobody has written down
hook: Two research fields can each hold half of an answer even when nobody has written the connection down.
simple: Literature-based discovery looks for useful links between separate bodies of research. The facts can already be public; the missing thing is the bridge.
why_interesting: Some unknowns are not missing facts. They are missing connections between facts that live in different vocabularies.
tangible_edge: This gives Unasked a practical search rule: when a question feels thin, do not just search harder inside the same field. Look for the field that already owns the other half of the problem.
why_here: Vocabulary trapdoor: a mature field for the problem of discovering things you do not yet know how to ask about.
confidence: high on the history of literature-based discovery; exploratory on the personal horizon-scanner application
